researchQuestion: Can an AI agent upgrade a vulnerable dependency without breaking the project?
studyLabel: A benchmark for fixing vulnerable dependencies in real projects while keeping the build and tests green
summary: VulnBump is 307 upgrade tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities in 43 repositories across six package managers, matched to Snyk Open Source production vulnerability distributions. An upgrade passes only if, in a fresh container, dependencies resolve, a rescan shows the targeted vulnerabilities fixed, the project builds, and every previously passing test still passes. All three agents use the same model, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and a non-agentic baseline that only applies Snyk's recommended version shows how much of the work that advice already does.

findings.title: Build and tests alone can't separate the agents; checking the fix does
findings.summary: On dependency resolution, build and tests, the three agents perform alike (92.8–93.8%). Once the rescan also checks the fix, Evo Remediation Agent passes 90.2% of upgrades, against 77.5% for Claude Code + Snyk scan and 59.6% for Claude Code unaided. Every pairwise difference between the agents is statistically significant.
findings.caveat: Each agent ran once per upgrade, and PASS does not penalise new vulnerabilities an upgrade pulls in, which appear more often for Evo Remediation Agent.

findings.title: An SCA scan is a key tool for agents fixing vulnerabilities
findings.summary: The Snyk Open Source scan and recommended upgrade raise Claude Code's PASS rate from 59.6% to 77.5%. Without them, Claude Code often picks a version Snyk still flags: 64 times, against 13 with the scan.
findings.caveat: Snyk is both the task source and the judge, so part of this gap may come from vulnerability databases disagreeing on which version fixes an issue.

findings.title: Same model, same findings: the harness makes the difference
findings.summary: On Claude Sonnet 5.5 with the same Snyk findings, Evo Remediation Agent's purpose-built harness passes 12.7 percentage points more than Claude Code + Snyk scan: 39 more upgrades, 23 of them major.
findings.caveat: All agents were tested with one model, Claude Sonnet 5.5. The setup compares complete systems and cannot isolate which part of the harness makes the difference.

findings.title: Claude Code fails silently; Evo Remediation Agent fails visibly
findings.summary: Claude Code often avoids the risky major upgrade, even when Snyk names the major target, and settles for a patch or minor version that leaves the vulnerability in place. In 70 of its 124 failures, Claude Code unaided reported vulnerabilities as fixed that the rescan still found. Evo Remediation Agent usually lands the upgrade, so most of its failures (21 of 30) break the build or tests, where the project's own checks catch them.
findings.caveat: Claude Code transcripts were not kept, and single repositories dominate some failure categories: one accounts for 28 of the 30 Claude Code dependency-gate failures.

findings.title: Major framework migrations remain hard for every agent
findings.summary: PASS rates fall from 96%, 88% and 70% on non-major upgrades to 81%, 61% and 42% on major ones for Evo Remediation Agent, Claude Code + Snyk scan and Claude Code unaided. 23 upgrades, mostly Spring, Spring Boot and Dropwizard migrations, defeat all three.
findings.caveat: The 23 unsolved upgrades come from just seven Maven and npm repositories.

findings.title: Transitive vulnerabilities are harder to fix for every harness
findings.summary: 70% of fixable vulnerabilities are transitive, arriving through packages the project does not declare directly, and for every harness, passing upgrades fix a smaller share of them than of direct ones. Snyk's guidance more than doubles the share of transitive vulnerabilities Claude Code fixes in passing upgrades, from 28% to 59%. Evo Remediation Agent fixes 73%.
findings.caveat: A vulnerability reachable through several upgrade paths counts as fixed only when every one of those upgrades removes its path.

methodology.title: Setup and baseline
methodology.text: The pinned repository is installed, scanned with snyk test, built and tested. Every Snyk fix group becomes one upgrade.
steps: Depth-1 clone of one pinned commit

methodology.title: Remediation
methodology.text: Once per upgrade, the agent edits a fresh copy of the repository in a sandbox; the package manager bump only applies Snyk's recommended version and refreshes the lockfile.
steps: Three agents, plus the package manager bump

methodology.title: Verification
methodology.text: A separate container applies four gates to the agent's working tree, without trusting anything the agent reports.

budgets.turns: All three agents use the same model and 110 agent turns per upgrade.

metrics.label: Dependencies resolve
metrics.description: The edited manifests and lockfiles install with the package manager's strict command, as CI would run it.

metrics.label: Targeted vulnerabilities fixed
metrics.description: A post-fix Snyk rescan of every target manifest no longer finds the targeted vulnerabilities through the upgraded package or any newly introduced dependency path.

metrics.label: Build
metrics.description: The project still compiles, type-checks, or imports its main package.

metrics.label: Tests pass
metrics.description: Every test that passed in the baseline still passes; a skipped or missing test is a regression.

metrics.label: Project still works
metrics.description: Dependencies, build and tests all pass, whether or not the vulnerability was fixed.

metrics.label: All gates pass (PASS)
metrics.description: All four gates pass: the vulnerability is fixed and the project still works.

metrics.label: Vulnerability instances fixed
metrics.description: Share of the fixable vulnerability instances fixed. An instance whose rescan failed counts as not fixed.

dimensions.label: Fix difficulty
dimensions.note: Smallest semantic-versioning jump from the installed version to a fixed release.

dimensions.label: Dependency type
dimensions.note: Whether the vulnerable package is declared in the manifest (direct) or arrives through another package (transitive).

qualitySignals.label: False fix claims
qualitySignals.description: Attempts where the agent said it fixed a vulnerability that the rescan still found.

qualitySignals.label: Attempts with new vulnerabilities
qualitySignals.description: Attempts whose post-fix scan shows vulnerability instances that were not in the baseline. PASS does not penalise them.

qualitySignals.label: New vulnerability instances
qualitySignals.description: Summed over attempts (critical / high / medium / low), which overcounts unique instances because upgrades in the same repository often introduce the same one.

qualitySignals.label: Fixable instances remaining
qualitySignals.description: Fixable instances not fixed, failed rescans included (critical / high / medium / low).

qualitySignals.label: Vulnerabilities moved
qualitySignals.description: Remaining instances that now arrive through a direct dependency that did not carry them in the baseline.

qualitySignals.label: Tests modified
qualitySignals.description: Attempts that edited test files. Agents may adapt tests to breaking changes, but must not edit them to make them pass.

qualitySignals.label: Unrelated bumps
qualitySignals.description: Attempts that bumped a direct dependency outside the fix's lane. Recorded, not failed.

qualitySignals.label: Unverified instances
qualitySignals.description: Remaining instances that only a failed rescan reports.

qualitySignals.label: Rescan failed
qualitySignals.description: Attempts whose verification rescan failed. They count as failures.

qualitySignals.label: Turn budget exhausted
qualitySignals.description: Attempts that used their whole turn budget.

qualitySignals.label: Timed out
qualitySignals.description: Attempts stopped at the wall-clock budget. They would count as failures.

qualitySignals.label: .snyk policy edits
qualitySignals.description: Attempts that added or edited a .snyk file. Both scans ignore policy, so this cannot hide a vulnerability.

qualitySignals.label: Infrastructure errors
qualitySignals.description: The agent never started, or the container ran out of memory. Excluded from every rate.

configurations.label: Claude Code unaided
configurations.subtitle: No target, Snyk blocked
configurations.description: Claude Code 2.1.289 given the same prompt without the target version ("Upgrade X to fix these vulnerabilities:") and no Snyk access, so it must find a fixed version itself, for example from OSV.

configurations.label: Claude Code + Snyk scan
configurations.subtitle: Given Snyk target + CLI
configurations.description: Claude Code 2.1.289 prompted with the upgrade's "Upgrade X to Y to fix" block from the baseline Snyk report, which names the target version, and the project's test command. It may run snyk test.

configurations.label: Evo Remediation Agent
configurations.subtitle: Snyk agentic remediation
configurations.description: Snyk's agentic remediation engine (snyk fix --agentic), run once per upgrade with the ids of the vulnerabilities it fixes. It leverages Snyk intelligence, which evolved from Snyk's deterministic SCA fix engine, runs its own scan, the build and tests, and repairs errors before finishing.

citation.title: VulnBump: A Benchmark for Fixing Vulnerable Dependencies in Real Projects While Keeping the Build and Tests Green

sources.label: Popular open-source projects
sources.description: Curated applications, frameworks, starters and tutorials for Gradle, npm, Yarn, pip and Poetry.

sources.label: GitHub searches for vulnerable packages
sources.description: Manifests that pin known-vulnerable versions of frequently vulnerable packages, plus searches for the less-represented package managers.

sources.label: BUMP projects
sources.description: Maven projects from the BUMP benchmark, pinned at the parent of a breaking-update commit, where the project still builds and passes its tests.

sources.label: Gradle submodules
sources.description: Modules of large multi-project builds, scanned separately so that one task does not span hundreds of modules.

sources.label: Popular Maven projects
sources.description: Top-starred on GitHub, pinned at their last commit before 21 May 2022, CORAL's snapshot date.

selection.selectionNote: Selected to match Snyk production data in direct versus transitive share, vulnerabilities per repository, severity and fix difficulty. Package managers are weighted so that each has enough cases to report on, rather than strictly in proportion to production.
selection.excludedReason: A few very large repositories, such as Apache Kafka and Spring Framework, were excluded because in earlier runs they ran out of memory or time, or had hundreds of upgrades that would take days to evaluate one by one. VulnBump therefore under-represents very large repositories and, since several are Gradle builds, Gradle.

representativeness.source: Snyk Open Source production findings in monitored projects, April–September 2026 (about 300,000 organisations and 459 million unique issue–project pairs), against the 43 VulnBump repositories, where vulnerabilities are counted once per project and vulnerability id.

dimensions.label: Direct dependency share
dimensions.note: Share of findings whose vulnerable package is declared in the manifest. Production comes from a 1% random sample of projects (4.2 million findings).

dimensions.label: Fix difficulty
dimensions.note: Smallest semantic-versioning jump to a fixed release. Production covers Java, JavaScript and Python findings (patch/minor/major 40/33/26% in Java, 27/48/25% in JavaScript, 21/50/29% in Python).

perProject.label: Vulnerabilities per project
perProject.note: Bar: P25 to P75 · tick: median · whiskers: P10 to P90.

deviations: Gradle is under-represented (3% of vulnerabilities against 17%), with a lower direct share (11% against 19%). Most Gradle candidates failed the filters, and the largest that qualified were too large to evaluate.
pip vulnerabilities are mostly direct (84% against 56%), because only three pip repositories qualified.

jumpCategories.label: Minor (0.x)
jumpCategories.note: Semantic versioning gives no compatibility guarantee below 1.0.

rootCauses.note: One root cause per failed attempt, grouped by cause rather than by first failed gate, so counts can differ from the first failed gates above.

groups.label: Version compatibility
groups.description: The new versions violate a version the project pins or requires: a dependency's declared range, the interpreter or the compiler.

groups.label: Code compatibility
groups.description: A changed API or behaviour breaks the project.

causes.label: Class or method missing at runtime

groups.label: Other
groups.description: A package removed from PyPI, a source build failure and a failed rescan.

rows.name: DepBench
rows.note: Held-out upgrade tests hidden from the agent.

rows.name: VulnBump
rows.ecosystems: Maven, Gradle, npm, Yarn, pip, Poetry

relatedWork.note: Vuln means a rescan with a production SCA scanner. Partial: dependencies checked only inside the Maven build (BUMP, BigBag, CORAL), in one combined install, build and test command (DepBench), or not scored separately (REQBench); build only as part of running the tests (DepRepair, DepBench) or a script (REQBench); tests only breakage-related ones (DepRepair) or a README script (REQBench); CVEs counted against the authors' own CVE-to-version mapping (CORAL). LADU builds and tests inside its agent loop but scores only overlap with manual upgrades. BUMP defines no repair scoring; its marks reflect the command used to reproduce each update.

baseline.label: Package manager bump
baseline.subtitle: Snyk's version, no agent
baseline.description: The non-agentic baseline: applies Snyk's recommended upgrade and nothing else. It uses no model, edits no code or tests, and never tries another version.
